processing: A boiled dish rather than a processed tea: black tea is simmered in a little water, then brought to the boil with plenty of milk and salt, and finished in the bowl with fat, black pepper and torn flatbread.
harvest_season: No harvest of its own: it uses everyday black tea and is made year-round, mainly for breakfast.
appearance_dry: Ordinary black tea leaf, only a small amount of it.
appearance_liquor: Opaque, milky beige, with melted fat on the surface and pieces of bread in the bowl.
appearance_wet: Not a feature of the dish: the small amount of leaf disappears into the milk.
taste_profile: Salty, rich and milky rather than tea-forward, with the warmth of black pepper and the weight of rendered fat and soaked bread.

brewing.notes: Boil half a teaspoon of black tea for 2 to 3 minutes in 50 to 75 g of water, add 400 to 500 g of milk and half a teaspoon of salt, and bring to the boil. In the bowl add fat, black pepper and torn flatbread, then rest about 5 minutes.

vintage_note: Never sold as a tea product or by year: it is made fresh in the kitchen from ordinary black tea, milk and salt. Any plain black tea works, as nothing about the dish depends on a harvest.
description:
Shirchoy is a salted milk tea of Central Asia that eats like a meal: black tea, milk and salt in a bowl with fat, pepper and torn flatbread. The name means milk tea, from Tajik shir and choy. In Uzbekistan it is especially associated with Tajik communities and with Bukhara and Samarkand; it is also popular among Karakalpaks and drunk in the Pamirs and Afghanistan.

The method is quick. A little black tea boils for a few minutes in a small amount of water, then milk and salt go in and the pot comes back to the boil. The fat, most often rendered tail fat of the Hissar sheep, goes into the traditional bowl called a kosa, along with pepper and bread.

The tea is really the background here. The bowl rests about five minutes so the bread soaks up milk and fat, and traditionally you eat the contents by hand. Think of it as a savoury breakfast, or occasionally a light supper, not as something to sip for its leaf.

There is nothing special to buy. Use plain black tea, whole milk and good fat, and add salt with care. If you want to explore this family further, Tibetan and Mongolian salted teas are close relatives under other names.
history:
Shirchoy is documented as a traditional dish of the Central Asian region, with close relatives in Mongolia and Tibet under other names. No inventor or starting date is recorded.

The best-known story concerns Bukhara: the last emir, Said Mir Mohammed Alim Khan, is said to have always begun breakfast with it, as local tradition required, which is taken as a sign that the dish crossed the line between rich and poor. The spelling varies, and it is also found as shirchai or shurchai, the last linked to the Persian word for salty.
